9702-9.1.1.motivate: What actually crosses a wire section when a lamp lights? Thinking in terms of moving particles makes current measurable.
9702-9.1.1.establish: An electric current is a flow of charge carriers. In a metal, free electrons move; in an electrolyte, positive and negative ions can move. A neutron has no charge, so a moving neutron alone does not carry electric current. Current describes charge flow, although the circuit can also transfer energy.
9702-9.1.1.connect: This idea lets us count the charge passing a section and then relate that count to time.
9702-9.1.1.note:
- Electric current: flow of charge carriers.
- Metal: free electrons; electrolyte: ions.
- Uncharged particles alone carry no current.
9702-9.1.1.self_explain: Why can an ion beam carry current but a neutron beam cannot?

9702-9.1.2.motivate: Oil droplets do not pick up arbitrary amounts of charge. Their measured charges occur in discrete steps.
9702-9.1.2.establish: Charge on a charge carrier is quantised: it is an integer multiple of the elementary charge $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$. Positive and negative multiples are possible, as is zero. Divide a proposed charge by $e$; the result must be an integer. For example, $4.8\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C=3e$ is possible, whereas $4.0\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C=2.5e$ is not.
9702-9.1.2.connect: The elementary charge also lets us convert between a number of electrons and total charge.
9702-9.1.2.note:
- Carrier charge is an integer multiple of $e$.
- $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$.
- Test a proposed charge by dividing by $e$.
9702-9.1.2.self_explain: Why is $-3.2\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$ possible but $+4.0\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$ impossible?

9702-9.1.3.motivate: To compare charge flow in two circuits, count how much charge passes a section in the same time.
9702-9.1.3.establish: For a constant current, $Q=It$: charge $Q$ in coulombs equals current $I$ in amperes multiplied by time $t$ in seconds. One coulomb is the charge transferred by one ampere in one second. Rearrange to $I=Q/t$ or $t=Q/I$ as required. If $N$ carriers each have charge magnitude $q$, then $Q=Nq$; for electrons $q=e$. In steady series flow, equal charge passes each section in the same time.
9702-9.1.3.connect: Combining $Q=It$ with the number of carriers crossing a conductor leads to the drift relation.
9702-9.1.3.note:
- $Q=It$ for constant current.
- $1\,\mathrm C$ passes with $1\,\mathrm A$ for $1\,\mathrm s$.
- For $N$ electrons, $Q=Ne$.
9702-9.1.3.self_explain: If a wire becomes narrower, why does the charge crossing each section in one second stay the same?

9702-9.1.4.motivate: Electrons drift slowly through a wire, yet a measurable current flows because so many electrons cross each section.
9702-9.1.4.establish: For a current-carrying conductor, $I=Anvq$, where $A$ is cross-sectional area, $n$ is the number density of charge carriers (number per unit volume), $v$ is average drift speed, and $q$ is the magnitude of charge per carrier. In time $t$, carriers travel $vt$ and sweep volume $Avt$. This contains $nAvt$ carriers, whose charge magnitude is $Q=nAvtq$. Since $I=Q/t$, $I=Anvq$. At fixed current in the same material, $v$ is inversely proportional to $A$.
9702-9.1.4.connect: The equation predicts that a narrow section has faster drift without any change in steady current.
9702-9.1.4.note:
- $n$ counts carriers per unit volume, in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$.
- Swept volume in time $t$ is $Avt$.
- $I=Anvq$; at fixed $I,n,q$, $v\propto1/A$.
9702-9.1.4.self_explain: Why does doubling wire diameter quarter the drift speed at the same current and material?
